You are interviewing for a Product Analyst role at Meta. North-star engagement dropped 8% week-over-week after a feed ranking change. What metrics would you inspect first, and how would you decide whether to roll back?

I would treat this as a possible causal effect of the ranking change, not just a dashboard dip. First I would confirm the drop is real: check instrumentation, traffic mix, and whether the decline is concentrated in the treatment cohort if this shipped as an A/B test. Then I would look at the north-star's inputs — time spent, sessions, and content diversity — plus guardrails like report rate and hide rate. If the experiment is still running I would estimate the average treatment effect with a CUPED-adjusted comparison and check heterogeneity by new vs. existing users. If the launch was a full rollout I would use a difference-in-differences against a holdout or a comparable surface, and I would roll back if the negative effect is statistically and practically meaningful with no offsetting long-term quality gain.

text: Next asker: alex

A teammate claims a new onboarding tooltip caused a 12% lift in day-7 retention because retention rose after launch. What threats to validity do you see, and how would you design a study that could actually support a causal claim?

A simple before-after comparison is not causal. Seasonality, a concurrent marketing campaign, or a change in the new-user mix could all explain the 12% lift. I would also worry about anticipation effects and about users who never saw the tooltip being pooled with those who did. To support a causal claim I would run a randomized experiment with a persisted control, pre-register day-7 retention as the primary metric, and use CUPED with pre-period activity to reduce variance. If randomization is impossible I would use a staggered rollout and a difference-in-differences design, testing parallel trends and showing that late cohorts were not already improving. I would also estimate the local effect among users who were actually shown the tooltip, not just an intent-to-treat average if assignment and exposure differ.

reason: Could have tied the design back to a product ship / no-ship recommendation more sharply.
